                   CARPENTER LAND AND CATTLE CO.’S REPLY BRIEF

         Carpenter Land and Cattle Co. (Carpenter) files this Reply Brief, and reaffirms that if the

  Honorable Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) and the Public Utility Commission of Texas

  (Commission) are inclined to determine that the Applicants have introduced evidence to

  sufficiently prove the public necessity for the proposed project, that it only approve the project if

  it can do so by approving a route for the proposed line that does not materially damage the use and

  enjoyment of the Texas State Parks and the Colorado River. Pursuant to SOAH Order No. 32,

  addressing post-hearing matters, this Reply Brief is timely filed on or before June 26, 2026.


                                        I.   INTRODUCTION


         The initial briefs filed in this case make clear that this study area is not comprised of one

  community but instead is characterized by essentially 4 general communities that are all of a

  different nature and character:
                                                                                                   Page 3 of 19


                Eastern – the portion of the study area in Bell and Williamson counties is in
                 transition to a suburban area characterized by many developers or properties that
                 either have are about to be in development;

                Burnet County – which is bounded by the Colorado River to the West and the
                 Lampasas River to the northeast;

                Central – bounded by the Colorado River to the east and spanning across San Saba
                 to the San Saba River and Menard Counties; and

                Western – Comprised of McCullough and Schleicher Counties where some of the
                 land has been developed for energy production.

        Carpenter will reply to varying extent to the initial briefs of parties within each of these

communities as they reflect on the Burnet county community to which Carpenter belongs. In the

interest of judicial efficiency in avoiding repetition and out of respect for the ALJs’ time, rather

than duplicating replies to initial briefs regarding the Colorado River crossings, prudent avoidance,

community values, and environmental integrity related to Routes 296, 572, and 894, the Reply

Brief of Save the Lampasas is incorporated by reference to Carpenter’s Reply Brief.

        Many of the parties supporting Route 894 are members of the communities of Williamson

and Bell counties and their positions address the impacts of Route 894 in that portion of the study

area.1 For those parties, Route 572 is identical to Route 894 in Bell and Williamson counties and

adoption of that route would be consistent with their positions.2 As indicated by the support of

Route 572, Carpenter does not oppose using the Links that comprise Route 894, or any of the other

Routes of Interest, in Williamson and Bell Counties (eastern corridors) so long as the links do not

                                       II.    ROUTING CRITERIA


          As indicated in the Initial Brief of Carpenter and those of many others, the Colorado River

crossings is a critical decision in the selection of a route in this proceeding. However, the record

demonstrates that Route 894, which crosses the Colorado River on Link J22, is not a reasonable

place to cross the Colorado River when other disturbed crossing locations already exist outside of

the viewshed of Post Oak State Park and Colorado Bend State Park.4




         3

         To date, no party has offered evidence in the record supporting J22 at the best performing

Colorado River crossing when considering the statutory factors of community values, parks and

recreational areas, environment, or aesthetics. Nor does any party challenge the recommendations

from TPWD that object to crossing at J11, J22, and J26 because of the negative impacts to the

viewshed of Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park.5 Instead, proponents of

Route 894 dismiss the importance of the undeniable damage to Colorado River, Greenwood Creek,

and the properties on its banks that would be fragmented by Link J22 that run counter to the

TPWD’s recommendations based on the form of their advocacy and on the fact that the Applicant

chose not to apply the recommendations in designating Route 894 in the Commission-prescribed

application form aa the “best meets” route.6 These parties place undue weight on the best meets

designation in the Application. As stated in the Applicants’ Initial Brief:

                    . . .To be clear, however, while the Applicants are required in the
                    Commission’s CCN application form to identify such a route, it is
                    the prerogative of the Commission to select a route for construction
                    of the Project in this proceeding.


                    Route selection under PURA and the Commission’s rules requires a
                    reasoned and considered balancing of all applicable factors—it is
                    not a mathematical exercise.7 . . .



         Furthermore, the parties advocating for crossing the Colorado River at J22 do so as part of

their support for Route 894 by relying heavily on assertions that the Route performs well

         A.         Best Alternate Routes Under PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)

                       1.       Community Values

         Many of the intervenors that support Route 894 do not challenge the concerns regarding

the impacts to the Colorado River, but instead offer myopic reference to the data in the Applicants

routing table that identifies only links that have parks within 0.5 miles of the boundaries of a state

park.9    This measurement fails to recognize that in addition to Link J22 negatively impacting

Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park and overall a poor location for the

Colorado River crossing, it is also coupled with negative impacts on the community values of

area.10This mathematical exercise also does not take into account the impacts to the Greenwood

Creek Ranch which includes Colorado River Frontage traversed by Link J22, with spectacular

views from the Main Lodge, proximity to the Greenwood Creek and surrounding natural springs

and pools; and the Mountain Top Lookout—a defining feature, the preservation of which is a core

value to Carpenter Family for the last 100 years.11

        The Initial Briefs of several parties focus their opposition to Route 296 on discussions of

community impacts to Florence Elementary School on Link F34.12 As discussed below, the

potential impact on this structure can be mitigated without the bounds of this case, and should not

serve to eliminate routing options that avoid running contrary to Commission precedent by

materially impacting the community’s enjoyment of the Colorado River at Greenwood Creek

Ranch nor should it result in selection of a route that impairs the public use of the Colorado Bend

and Post Oak Ridge State Parks.

                      2.        Recreational and Park Areas

        Carpenter agrees with the intervenors that recognize that “State Parks are significant

resources [that are] visited by thousands of Texans every year”13 and endorse the arguments that

consider both J11 and J26 poor choices to cross the Colorado River given that their concerns should

apply equally to the crossing at Link J22.14 Despite the importance of State Parks, some parties’

attempt to dismiss the devastating impacts to the Colorado River and Colorado Bend State and

Post Oak Ridge State Parkes by turning to two linear distance measurements in EA Table 7-2: (1)

“Length of route across parks/recreational areas” and (2) “Estimated length of right-of-way within

foreground visual zone of park/recreational areas.”15 The record evidence makes clear that the

Applicants’ consultant used a linear distance from the park boundaries to calculate the visual

foreground (metric (2)).16 However, neither of these numbers accurately captures the impacts of

relevant to the ultimate consideration of community values, recreational and park areas, aesthetics

and environmental integrity.

       As indicated by the TPWD’s response to the Applicant’s Agency Notice Letter, a “150 to

200-foot-tall transmission line and tower within 5 miles of a scenic viewpoint valued for its natural

qualities, is likely to be distracting to most visitors.17 This distance is within the foreground–

middle ground where form, line, color, and texture contrasts are most apparent to the casual

observer.”18 Therefore, not only do the M31, M32, andM33 Opposition Landowners

mischaracterize the TPWD’s involvement in this proceeding,19 but many others also overlook the

TPWD’s foreground-middle ground recommendations that are specific in their concerns regarding

J22.20 In fact, TPWD provided two recommendations to protect State Park viewsheds in this

proceeding, No. 2 reads “Coordinate with TPWD to expand buffer up to 5 miles on TPWD

properties known for their natural quality and scenic viewpoints (Table)” and No. 3 reads

“Mitigate impacts by avoiding ridgelines and hilltops near TPWD properties of interest, avoid

lighting and reflective materials, installing vegetative screening, staggered plantings in ROW, and

other efforts per the BLMs Visual Resource Management Manual.”21

would be 0.6 miles from Post Oak State Park and would cross over the highest point on the property

                       3.      Aesthetic and Historic Values

                                 a.       Aesthetic

         In discussing aesthetic impacts, other intervenors support Route 894 for its visibility

metrics (i.e., less visibility from roads and highways) by relying on the numerical line items in the

Applicants’ data tables. However, Route 296 is in the viewshed of more miles of roads and

highways because it parallels more roads and highways than 894 (14.84 mi. for 296 and only 4.45

mi. for 894).30 The tradeoff is not in the aesthetics metric, it is in parallelling, which supports the

selection of Route 296. Under this approach, other Initial Briefs acknowledge that Route 572

performs better on the aesthetic metrics than Route 894.

         Furthermore, while aesthetics is important along the entire 200+ miles of the study area, it

is a concern in rural, undisturbed areas, especially those dedicated to State Parks. As discussed

above, the metric reflected in the Applicants’ data table does not properly measure the aesthetic

impacts to the State Parks associated with the Colorado River Crossing. Route 894, which uses

Link J22, has negative aesthetic impacts to these State Parks which should be considered by the

ALJs and Commission with the same reverence as Link J11 and J26. Further, these Initial Briefs

supporting Route 894 do not address the fact that this Link traverses a higher elevation area on the

J22 would be seen clearly from the State Park and the River, even at a distance. Both the proximity

to the Park(s) issue (i.e., Links J11, J22, and J26) and the proximate viewshed issue (i.e., Link

J22), can be avoided by crossing the Colorado River at Link J31.32 This would also alleviate the

negative aesthetic impacts to the historic Greenwood Creek Ranch. This is coupled with the fact

that this crossing is already near a disturbed corridor because it is within 1,200 feet of a pipeline

crossing.33

potential.”34 As indicated by intervenors at the Hearing on the Merits and the Initial Briefs, this

                            4. Environmental Integrity

        Because Route 296 and Route 894 cross the same study area and are similar in length, they

have very similar environmental numbers in the tables presented with the (i.e., riparian areas,

wetlands, open waters, etc.).39 However, evaluation of the comparative environmental impacts

cannot be gleaned from these linear numbers.

        In this case, the environmental evaluation requires a review of link-specific and property-

specific attributes, such as the Colorado River crossing at an undisturbed area, the Greenwood

Creek and surrounding tributaries, springs, and pools present on Link J22, the Panther Creek

Wildlife Management Association area, and the Golden-Cheeked-warblers identified on the

G51/G52 corridor.40 Proponents of Route 894 argue that it avoids Link J31 and its “documented

golden-cheeked-warbler habitat;”41 however, the evidence makes clear that there is other

documented golden-cheeked-warblers present on Greenwood Creek Ranch documented through

its wildlife management program.42 These ecosystems and features will be in jeopardy if Route

894 is selected.

        The Mosley Group also mischaracterizes key environmental facts about Link J22 that must

be clarified: J22 sits between two bends in the Colorado River, it crosses Greenwood Creek twice,

runs through a ranch with documented golden-cheeked-warblers, has a turning structure at the

                              5. Prudent Avoidance

           As the Applicants point out, each of the routes comply with the Commission’s standards

for prudent avoidance. Despite this, some Initial Briefs argue that Route 296 should be removed

from consideration because of 2 habitable structures that are within the notice distance of the

centerline of Link F34. However, Commission precedent is clear that a school or a church in the

notice distance are not a basis for route disqualification.44                However, if the ALJs and the

Commission are inclined that the Florence ISD school within the notice distance is determinative,

the ALJs and the Commission can approve modifications in this case to place Link F34 farther

from these two specific structures to alleviate such concerns on noticed property.45 Further, neither

of these structures are present on Route 572 or the eastern portion of 894.46 As a result, the selection

of Route 572 or a combination of 894 (east) and 296 (west) route /of the above-mentioned

structures that more specifically characterized after Link F34 was determined.47

                                                    V.    PERMITS

       The Applicants confirmed that the possibility of many regulatory hurdles upon selection of

a route in this proceeding.55 They specifically acknowledged that a Section 404 Clean Water Permit

and consultation with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers remains a possibility depending on the

route selected by the Commission and the specific attributes of the links that make up the route. 56

Beyond this general acknowledgement, the Applicants did not alleviate any concerns about the
